claim: MicroRNAs (miRNAs) direct post-transcriptional regulation of human genes by guiding Argonaute proteins to complementary sites in messenger RNAs (mRNAs) targeted for repression.
source: MicroRNAs (miRNAs) direct post-transcriptional regulation of human genes by guiding Argonaute proteins to complementary sites in messenger RNAs (mRNAs) targeted for repression.
evidence: This is a well-established concept in the field, supported by the general knowledge of miRNA function.

claim: An adenosine (A) nucleotide opposite miRNA nucleotide-1 confers enhanced target repression independently of base pairing potential to the miRNA in many conserved mammalian miRNA target sites.
source: An enigmatic feature of many conserved mammalian miRNA target sites is that an adenosine (A) nucleotide opposite miRNA nucleotide-1 confers enhanced target repression independently of base pairing potential to the miRNA.
evidence: This statement references established observations in the field about t1A nucleotides.

claim: Human Argonaute2 (Ago2) possesses a solvated surface pocket that specifically binds adenine nucleobases in the t1 position of target RNAs.
source: In this study, we show that human Argonaute2 (Ago2) possesses a solvated surface pocket that specifically binds adenine nucleobases in the 1 position (t1) of target RNAs.
evidence: This claim is supported by the crystal structures and binding experiments presented in the manuscript.

claim: t1A nucleotides are recognized indirectly through a hydrogen-bonding network of water molecules that preferentially interacts with the N6 amine on adenine.
source: t1A nucleotides are recognized indirectly through a hydrogen-bonding network of water molecules that preferentially interacts with the N6 amine on adenine.
evidence: This is supported by the crystal structures showing ordered water molecules and binding experiments with modified nucleotides.

claim: t1A nucleotides are not utilized during the initial binding of Ago2 to its target, but instead function by increasing the dwell time on target RNA.
source: t1A nucleotides are not utilized during the initial binding of Ago2 to its target, but instead function by increasing the dwell time on target RNA.
evidence: This is supported by single-molecule FRET experiments showing similar association rates but different dwell times.

claim: N6 adenosine methylation blocks t1A recognition.
source: We also show that N6 adenosine methylation blocks t1A recognition, revealing a possible mechanism for modulation of miRNA target site potency.
evidence: This is supported by binding experiments with m6A-modified target RNAs.

claim: Over two thousand unique human miRNA sequences have been reported.
source: Over two thousand unique human miRNA sequences have been reported and more than half of all protein-coding human genes are predicted to contain a conserved miRNA recognition site (Friedman et al., 2009; Kozomara and Griffiths-Jones, 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: More than half of all protein-coding human genes are predicted to contain a conserved miRNA recognition site.
source: Over two thousand unique human miRNA sequences have been reported and more than half of all protein-coding human genes are predicted to contain a conserved miRNA recognition site (Friedman et al., 2009; Kozomara and Griffiths-Jones, 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: miRNAs function as guides for Argonaute proteins, which use the sequence information encoded in each miRNA to identify complementary sites in mRNAs targeted for repression.
source: miRNAs function as guides for Argonaute proteins, which use the sequence information encoded in each miRNA to identify complementary sties in mRNAs targeted for repression (Liu et al., 2004; Meister et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Argonautes recruit additional silencing factors that mediate translational repression and degradation of the targeted mRNAs.
source: Argonautes then recruit additional silencing factors that mediate translational repression and degradation of the targeted mRNAs (Huntzinger and Izaurralde, 2011).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: Perfect complementarity between miRNAs and their targets is not necessary for silencing.
source: Pioneering studies in the nematode Caenorhabditis elegans showed that perfect complementarity between miRNAs and their targets is not necessary for silencing (Lee et al., 1993; Wightman et al., 1993).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Base pairing interactions with nucleotides towards the 5′ end of the miRNA are particularly important for target recognition.
source: Examination of regulatory elements in fly mRNAs then revealed a striking degree of complementarity to the 5′ ends of subset of conserved miRNAs, suggesting that base paring interactions with nucleotides towards the 5′ end of the miRNA are particularly important for target recognition (Lai, 2002).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: Pairing to the miRNA 'seed region' (nt 2–7 or 2–8, from the miRNA 5′ end) is the most evolutionarily conserved feature of miRNA targets in animals.
source: Indeed, phylogenetic analysis showed that pairing to the miRNA 'seed region' (nt 2–7 or 2–8, from the miRNA 5′ end) is the most evolutionarily conserved feature of miRNA targets in animals (Lewis et al., 2003; Brennecke et al., 2005; Krek et al., 2005; Lewis et al., 2005)
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Complementarity to the miRNA seed is generally sufficient to elicit significant levels of target recognition and repression.
source: and complementarity to the miRNA seed is generally sufficient to elicit significant levels of target recognition and repression (Doench and Sharp, 2004; Brennecke et al., 2005; Lim et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: An adenosine (A) nucleotide opposite miRNA nucleotide-1 is a conserved feature of many vertebrate miRNA target sites.
source: Careful comparison of miRNA seed-matched sites in the 3′ untranslated regions (UTRs) of human, mouse, rat, dog, and chicken genomes also revealed that an adenosine (A) nucleotide opposite miRNA nucleotide-1 is a conserved feature of many vertebrate miRNA target sites (Lewis et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: t1A nucleotides confer enhanced repression of miRNA targets beyond pairing to the seed region alone.
source: These t1A nucleotides confer enhanced repression of miRNA targets beyond pairing to the seed region alone (Grimson et al., 2007; Nielsen et al., 2007; Baek et al., 2008; Selbach et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: t1A nucleotides function independently of the identity of miRNA nucleotide-1.
source: Curiously, unlike the seed-matched region, t1A nucleotides function independently of the identity of miRNA nucleotide-1, indicating that t1A recognition occurs through a mechanism that is distinct from base pairing with the miRNA guide (Grimson et al., 2007; Nielsen et al., 2007; Baek et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: t1A recognition occurs through a mechanism that is distinct from base pairing with the miRNA guide.
source: Curiously, unlike the seed-matched region, t1A nucleotides function independently of the identity of miRNA nucleotide-1, indicating that t1A recognition occurs through a mechanism that is distinct from base pairing with the miRNA guide (Grimson et al., 2007; Nielsen et al., 2007; Baek et al., 2008).
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that t1A function is independent of miRNA nucleotide-1 identity, supported by citations.

claim: Ago2 cradles the duplex formed by miRNA nucleotides 2–7 and the complementary target RNA.
source: These structures revealed that Ago2 cradles the duplex formed by miRNA nucleotides 2–7 and the complementary target RNA, explaining why seed pairing is critical for recognition of miRNA target sites (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is supported by crystal structures reported in the manuscript.

claim: Seed pairing is critical for recognition of miRNA target sites.
source: These structures revealed that Ago2 cradles the duplex formed by miRNA nucleotides 2–7 and the complementary target RNA, explaining why seed pairing is critical for recognition of miRNA target sites (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is explained by the structural data showing how Ago2 interacts with the seed-paired duplex.

claim: t1A nucleotides interact with a surface pocket formed at the interface of the L2 and MID domains of Ago2.
source: We also noted that t1A nucleotides interact with a surface pocket formed at the interface of the L2 and MID domains of Ago2, and proposed that this additional interaction may contribute to the affinity of Ago2 for miRNA target sites.
evidence: This is based on previously reported crystal structures.

claim: The t1-nucleotide binding pocket is large enough to accommodate any of the four natural RNA bases.
source: However, the t1-nucleotide binding pocket is large enough to accommodate any of the four natural RNA bases, and the contacts between Ago2 and t1A appear to be almost entirely non-specific (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is based on structural observations from crystal structures.

claim: The contacts between Ago2 and t1A appear to be almost entirely non-specific.
source: However, the t1-nucleotide binding pocket is large enough to accommodate any of the four natural RNA bases, and the contacts between Ago2 and t1A appear to be almost entirely non-specific (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is based on structural observations from crystal structures.

claim: The t1-nucleotide binding pocket in Ago2 preferentially interacts with A nucleotides through water-mediated contacts to adenosine N6 amine.
source: In this study, we show that the t1-nucleotide binding pocket in Ago2 preferentially interacts with A nucleotides through water-mediated contacts to adenosine N6 amine.
evidence: This is supported by crystal structures and binding experiments presented in the manuscript.

claim: Adding a methyl group to the t1A N6 amine reduces target affinity.
source: Adding a methyl group to the t1A N6 amine reduces target affinity, raising the possibility that adenosine methylation could, in principle, lead to partial derepression of miRNA targets containing 7mer-A1 or 8mer sites.
evidence: This is supported by binding experiments with m6A-modified target RNAs.

claim: Adenosine methylation could lead to partial derepression of miRNA targets containing 7mer-A1 or 8mer sites.
source: Adding a methyl group to the t1A N6 amine reduces target affinity, raising the possibility that adenosine methylation could, in principle, lead to partial derepression of miRNA targets containing 7mer-A1 or 8mer sites.
evidence: This is a speculative inference based on the observation that m6A reduces target affinity.

claim: t1A is not used in the initial search for target sites.
source: We also present data indicating that t1A is not used in the initial search for target sites, but instead provides an anchor that helps retain Ago2 on seed-matched sites on target RNAs.
evidence: This is supported by single-molecule FRET experiments showing similar association rates for different t1 nucleotides.

claim: t1A provides an anchor that helps retain Ago2 on seed-matched sites on target RNAs.
source: We also present data indicating that t1A is not used in the initial search for target sites, but instead provides an anchor that helps retain Ago2 on seed-matched sites on target RNAs.
evidence: This is supported by single-molecule FRET experiments showing increased dwell times for t1A targets.

claim: The overall conformation of Ago2 is nearly identical in structures with different t1 nucleotides.
source: The overall conformation of Ago2 is nearly identical in the four different t1 structures, indicating that identity of the t1 nucleotide does not affect the structure of the protein.
evidence: This is based on comparison of crystal structures with different t1 nucleotides.

claim: The identity of the t1 nucleotide does not affect the structure of Ago2.
source: The overall conformation of Ago2 is nearly identical in the four different t1 structures, indicating that identity of the t1 nucleotide does not affect the structure of the protein.
evidence: This is inferred from the structural similarity observed in crystal structures.

claim: Non-A t1 nucleotides (C, U, G) were mostly disordered in the crystal structures.
source: Inspection of target RNA omit maps, in which the target RNAs were excluded from refinement, revealed little or no well-defined electron density for all of the non-A nucleotides, indicating that the non-A t1 nucleotides were mostly disordered (Figure 2).
evidence: This is based on electron density maps from crystal structures.

claim: The target omit map from the t1A data set had clearly defined density for the t1A inside the t1-nucleotide binding pocket.
source: In contrast, the target omit map from the t1A data set had clearly defined density for the t1A inside the t1-nucleotide binding pocket.
evidence: This is based on electron density maps from crystal structures.

claim: t1G and t1C interactions do not contribute substantially to target affinity.
source: Moreover, although residual electron density was observed for t1G and t1C nucleotides, binding experiments using the same target RNAs show that these interactions do not contribute substantially to target affinity (Figure 2).
evidence: This is supported by binding experiments showing similar affinities for t1G, t1C, and t1U targets.

claim: Adenine is the only nucleobase that associates stably enough with the t1-binding site to contribute to overall target affinity.
source: We conclude that, although the t1-binding site is large enough to accommodate any of the four natural RNA bases, adenine is the only nucleobase that associates stably enough to contribute to overall target affinity.
evidence: This is concluded from structural and binding data showing specific recognition of adenine.

claim: The purine N6 amine is the major determinant for distinguishing the t1A purine ring from t1G.
source: We conclude that the purine N6 and N2 amines both have positive effects on t1-binding, and that the N6 amine is the major determinant for distinguishing the t1A purine ring from tG.
evidence: This is concluded from binding experiments with inosine and DAP nucleotides.

claim: The purine N6 and N2 amines both have positive effects on t1-binding.
source: We conclude that the purine N6 and N2 amines both have positive effects on t1-binding, and that the N6 amine is the major determinant for distinguishing the t1A purine ring from tG.
evidence: This is concluded from binding experiments with inosine and DAP nucleotides.

claim: Ago2 bound the t1I target with an affinity similar to t1G.
source: Ago2 bound the t1I target with an affinity similar to t1G (Table 2)
evidence: This is supported by binding experiments reported in Table 2.

claim: No electron density was observed for the t1I nucleotide in target omit maps.
source: and no electron density was observed for the t1I nucleotide target omit maps, indicating that removal of the guanine N2 amine is insufficient to promote interactions with the t1-binding site (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is based on electron density maps from crystal structures.

claim: Removal of the guanine N2 amine is insufficient to promote interactions with the t1-binding site.
source: and no electron density was observed for the t1I nucleotide target omit maps, indicating that removal of the guanine N2 amine is insufficient to promote interactions with the t1-binding site (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is inferred from the lack of electron density for t1I and its similar affinity to t1G.

claim: Unambiguous electron density was observed for the t1DAP nucleotide.
source: In contrast, we observed unambiguous electron density for the t1DAP nucleotide, which bound Ago2 in the same position and anti conformation as t1A (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is based on electron density maps from crystal structures.

claim: t1DAP bound Ago2 in the same position and anti conformation as t1A.
source: In contrast, we observed unambiguous electron density for the t1DAP nucleotide, which bound Ago2 in the same position and anti conformation as t1A (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is based on crystal structure analysis.

claim: The affinity of the t1DAP target is approximately 1.7-fold greater than that of the equivalent t1A target.
source: Moreover, the affinity of the t1DAP target is ∼1.7-fold greater than that of the equivalent t1A target, indicating that Ago2 has a modest, though significant, preference for t1DAP over t1A (p-value = 0.0025; two-tailed, unpaired Student's t-test).
evidence: This is supported by binding experiments and statistical analysis.

claim: Ago2 has a modest, though significant, preference for t1DAP over t1A.
source: Moreover, the affinity of the t1DAP target is ∼1.7-fold greater than that of the equivalent t1A target, indicating that Ago2 has a modest, though significant, preference for t1DAP over t1A (p-value = 0.0025; two-tailed, unpaired Student's t-test).
evidence: This is inferred from the binding affinity measurements.

claim: Adding a methyl group to the t1A N6 amine reduced target affinity to that of a non-t1A target.
source: Consistent with this idea, adding a methyl group to the t1A N6 amine reduced target affinity to that of a non-t1A target (Figure 3D).
evidence: This is supported by binding experiments with m6A-modified target RNAs.

claim: The only direct contact between the t1A N6 amine and Ago2 is a hydrogen bond to the side chain of Ser-561.
source: The only direct contact between the t1A N6 amine and Ago2 is a hydrogen bond to the side chain of Ser-561 (Figure 1).
evidence: This is based on crystal structure analysis.

claim: The serine alcohol can function as both a hydrogen bond acceptor and donor.
source: Because the serine alcohol can function as both a hydrogen bond acceptor and donor, it is unlikely that this interaction alone can discriminate a purine N6 amine from an O6 carbonyl.
evidence: This is based on established chemical knowledge about serine.

claim: The serine alcohol interaction alone is unlikely to discriminate a purine N6 amine from an O6 carbonyl.
source: Because the serine alcohol can function as both a hydrogen bond acceptor and donor, it is unlikely that this interaction alone can discriminate a purine N6 amine from an O6 carbonyl.
evidence: This is inferred from the chemical properties of serine.

claim: Four ordered water molecules in a hydrogen-bonding network could selectively interact with purine N6 amines.
source: However, examination of the solvent surrounding the t1A nucleobase identified four ordered water molecules in a hydrogen-bonding network that could selectively interact with purine N6 amines.
evidence: This is based on crystal structure analysis showing ordered water molecules.

claim: Ago2 uses main chain carbonyls inside the t1-binding pocket to direct the hydrogen atoms on water B away from the purine 6-position.
source: Thus, our model suggests that Ago2 uses main chain carbonyls inside the t1-binding pocket to direct the hydrogen atoms on water B away from the purine 6-position, leaving only lone pair electrons available for establishing interactions with t1 nucleotides.
evidence: This is a model proposed based on structural observations and hydrogen bonding geometry.

claim: The lone pair electrons on water B are positioned to accept a hydrogen bond from purine N6 amines and to repel O6 carbonyls.
source: In the proposed orientation, the lone pair electrons on water B are positioned to accept a hydrogen bond from purine N6 amines and to repel O6 carbonyls.
evidence: This is inferred from the proposed model of water orientation in the binding pocket.

claim: Waters C and D likely provide an additional layer of selectivity through interactions with the unprotonated N1 amine on t1A.
source: Waters 'C' and 'D' likely provide an additional layer of selectivity through interactions with the unprotonated N1 amine on t1A, and may interact with the purine N2 amine, which does not directly contact Ago2.
evidence: This is speculative inference based on the positions of water molecules in the structure.

claim: Waters C and D may interact with the purine N2 amine.
source: Waters 'C' and 'D' likely provide an additional layer of selectivity through interactions with the unprotonated N1 amine on t1A, and may interact with the purine N2 amine, which does not directly contact Ago2.
evidence: This is speculative inference based on the positions of water molecules in the structure.

claim: The A481T mutation was designed to disrupt the water network inside the t1-binding site.
source: We tested the role of water molecules in t1A recognition by designing a mutation in Ago2 that disrupts the water network inside the t1-binding site.
evidence: This is the stated rationale for the mutation experiment.

claim: The overall structure of A481T Ago2 is nearly identical to the wild type protein.
source: The overall structure of A481T Ago2 is nearly identical to the wild type protein, and the structure of the t1-binding pocket is almost completely unaffected by the A481T mutation.
evidence: This is based on comparison of crystal structures.

claim: The structure of the t1-binding pocket is almost completely unaffected by the A481T mutation.
source: The overall structure of A481T Ago2 is nearly identical to the wild type protein, and the structure of the t1-binding pocket is almost completely unaffected by the A481T mutation.
evidence: This is based on comparison of crystal structures.

claim: The A481T mutation adds a hydrogen-bond acceptor/donor to the back of the t1-binding pocket without otherwise perturbing the structure of Ago2.
source: Thus, the A481T mutation adds a hydrogen-bond acceptor/donor to the back of the t1-binding pocket without otherwise perturbing the structure of Ago2.
evidence: This is concluded from structural analysis of the mutant protein.

claim: t1A recognition is severely impaired in A481T Ago2.
source: Although the structure of the A481T Ago2 is nearly identical to wild type, t1A recognition is severely impaired.
evidence: This is supported by electron density maps and binding experiments.

claim: Only residual electron density was observed for the t1A nucleotide in the A481T Ago2 target RNA omit map.
source: Only residual electron density was observed for the t1A nucleotide in the target RNA omit map (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is based on electron density maps from crystal structures.

claim: The A481T Ago2 bound t1A and t1G target RNAs with nearly identical affinities.
source: Moreover, the A481T Ago2 bound t1A and t1G target RNAs with nearly identical affinities (Figure 5D).
evidence: This is supported by binding experiments.

claim: The Oγ hydroxyl of Thr-481 is 4.2 Å from the position of the t1A N6 amine in the wild-type structure.
source: Importantly, the Oγ hydroxyl of Thr-481 is 4.2 Å from the position of the t1A N6 amine in the wild-type structure, strongly indicating that the mutation affects t1A recognition indirectly (Figure 5E).
evidence: This is based on structural comparison.

claim: The A481T mutation affects t1A recognition indirectly.
source: Importantly, the Oγ hydroxyl of Thr-481 is 4.2 Å from the position of the t1A N6 amine in the wild-type structure, strongly indicating that the mutation affects t1A recognition indirectly (Figure 5E).
evidence: This is inferred from the distance between the mutation site and the t1A N6 amine.

claim: Binding specificity in the t1-pocket is achieved by Ago2-directed solvent interactions with the t1 adenosine.
source: We conclude that binding specificity in the t1-pocket is achieved by Ago2-directed solvent interactions with the t1 adenosine.
evidence: This is concluded from the structural and mutational analysis.

claim: Ago2 recognizes target RNAs with t1U, t1A, or t1DAP at similar rates.
source: Measuring the time of the first arrival revealed that Ago2 recognizes the three targets at similar rates (kon(obs) = 0.040 ± 0.009, 0.033 ± 0.004, and 0.041 ± 0.008 s−1 nM−1 for t1U, t1A, and t1DAP targets, respectively), demonstrating that t1-nucleotide identity has little, if any, effect on the association of Ago2 with target RNAs (Figure 6D).
evidence: This is supported by single-molecule FRET experiments.

claim: t1-nucleotide identity has little, if any, effect on the association of Ago2 with target RNAs.
source: Measuring the time of the first arrival revealed that Ago2 recognizes the three targets at similar rates (kon(obs) = 0.040 ± 0.009, 0.033 ± 0.004, and 0.041 ± 0.008 s−1 nM−1 for t1U, t1A, and t1DAP targets, respectively), demonstrating that t1-nucleotide identity has little, if any, effect on the association of Ago2 with target RNAs (Figure 6D).
evidence: This is concluded from the similar association rates observed in single-molecule experiments.

claim: The average dwell time of Ago2 on the t1A and t1DAP targets was more than threefold longer than on the t1U target.
source: In contrast, the average dwell time (Δτ) of Ago2 on the t1A and t1DAP targets was more than threefold longer than on the t1U target (Figure 6E).
evidence: This is supported by single-molecule FRET experiments.

claim: The Δτ distribution of t1U is well described by a single-exponential decay.
source: We note that, although the Δτ distribution of t1U is well described by a single-exponential decay (Δτ = 1.64 ± 0.11 s, R2 = 0.994), the Δτ distributions of t1A and t1DAP deviate noticeably from ideal (R2 = 0.972 and 0.961 for t1A and t1DAP, respectively; Figure 6E, gray lines).
evidence: This is based on statistical analysis of single-molecule FRET data.

claim: The Δτ distributions of t1A and t1DAP deviate noticeably from a single-exponential decay.
source: We note that, although the Δτ distribution of t1U is well described by a single-exponential decay (Δτ = 1.64 ± 0.11 s, R2 = 0.994), the Δτ distributions of t1A and t1DAP deviate noticeably from ideal (R2 = 0.972 and 0.961 for t1A and t1DAP, respectively; Figure 6E, gray lines).
evidence: This is based on statistical analysis of single-molecule FRET data.

claim: t1A and t1DAP binding events consist of at least two discrete populations.
source: This observation indicates that t1A and t1DAP binding events consist of at least two discrete populations.
evidence: This is inferred from the deviation from single-exponential decay.

claim: About half of the t1A and t1DAP binding events had dwell times closely matching that of the t1U target.
source: Assuming only two populations exist, we fit each data set to a double-exponential decay and calculated that about half of the binding events (49.8% ± 6.2% and 44.6% ± 4.4% for t1A and t1DAP, respectively) had dwell times closely matching that of the t1U target (Δτ1 (t1A) = 1.61 ± 0.29 s; Δτ1 (t1DAP) = 1.97 ± 0.24).
evidence: This is based on double-exponential fitting of single-molecule FRET data.

claim: The other half of t1A and t1DAP binding events had an average dwell time more than fivefold longer than t1U.
source: In contrast, the other half of the binding events had an average dwell time more than fivefold longer (Δτ2 (t1A) = 8.69 ± 0.45 s; Δτ2 (t1DAP) = 12.87 ± 0.47 s).
evidence: This is based on double-exponential fitting of single-molecule FRET data.

claim: When using limited seed-pairing, Ago2 dissociates from the target RNA without stably engaging t1A about half of the time.
source: The simplest explanation for these observations is that, when using limited seed-pairing as in our experimental setup, Ago2 dissociates from the target RNA without stably engaging t1A about half of the time.
evidence: This is inferred from the two populations of dwell times observed in single-molecule experiments.

claim: When Ago2 does engage t1A, the affinity of the interaction is increased substantially.
source: However, in cases in which Ago2 does engage t1A, the affinity of the interaction is increased substantially.
evidence: This is inferred from the longer dwell times observed for the second population in single-molecule experiments.

claim: t1A binding increases the dwell time on target RNAs by anchoring Ago2 to seed-paired target sites and inhibiting dissociation.
source: Based on this observation, we suggest that t1A binding increases the dwell time on target RNAs by anchoring Ago2 to seed-paired target sites and inhibiting dissociation.
evidence: This is inferred from the structural observation that t1A inserts at an angle orthogonal to the target RNA trajectory and the increased dwell times.

claim: Human Ago2 contains a t1-nucleotide binding pocket that specifically recognizes adenine nucleobases through water-mediated contacts.
source: In this study we provide evidence that human Ago2 contains a t1-nucleotide binding pocket that specifically recognizes adenine nucleobases through water-mediated contacts.
evidence: This is the main conclusion of the study, supported by structural and binding data.

claim: The mechanism of t1A recognition by Ago2 is reminiscent of interactions in the trp operator/repressor complex.
source: Our model is reminiscent of interactions in the trp operator/repressor complex, which also uses an ordered network of hydrogen-bonded water molecules to achieve nucleobase recognition (Otwinowski et al., 1988).
evidence: This is a comparison to a known system, supported by citation.

claim: The adenosine N6 amine is a key determinant of specificity in t1A recognition.
source: We also show that the adenosine N6 amine is a key determinant of specificity and that the addition of a methyl group to the N6 amine blocks t1A recognition.
evidence: This is supported by binding experiments with modified nucleotides.

claim: m6A modifications are enriched in mammalian mRNA 3′ UTRs.
source: Taken with the finding that m6A modifications are enriched in mammalian mRNA 3′ UTRs (Meyer et al., 2012), this result raises the intriguing possibility that, in some cases, miRNA targets may be partially derepressed via adenosine methylation at 7mer-A1 and 8mer sites (Bartel, 2009).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: In some cases, miRNA targets may be partially derepressed via adenosine methylation at 7mer-A1 and 8mer sites.
source: Taken with the finding that m6A modifications are enriched in mammalian mRNA 3′ UTRs (Meyer et al., 2012), this result raises the intriguing possibility that, in some cases, miRNA targets may be partially derepressed via adenosine methylation at 7mer-A1 and 8mer sites (Bartel, 2009).
evidence: This is a speculative inference based on the observation that m6A blocks t1A recognition and the enrichment of m6A in 3′ UTRs.

claim: The amino acids making up the t1-binding site in Ago2 are conserved in all four human Argonaute proteins.
source: The amino acids making up the t1-binding site in Ago2 are conserved in all four human Argonaute proteins, and the structure of the t1-binding pocket in Ago2 is nearly identical to the same region in the structure of human Ago1 (Faehnle et al., 2013; Nakanishi et al., 2013).
evidence: This is based on sequence conservation analysis and structural comparison.

claim: The structure of the t1-binding pocket in Ago2 is nearly identical to the same region in the structure of human Ago1.
source: The amino acids making up the t1-binding site in Ago2 are conserved in all four human Argonaute proteins, and the structure of the t1-binding pocket in Ago2 is nearly identical to the same region in the structure of human Ago1 (Faehnle et al., 2013; Nakanishi et al., 2013).
evidence: This is based on structural comparison, supported by citations.

claim: Two ordered water molecules corresponding to waters A and B were observed in the structure of human Ago1 crystallized in the absence of target RNA.
source: In fact, two ordered water molecules corresponding to waters A and B were observed in the structure of human Ago1 crystallized in the absence of target RNA (Nakanishi et al., 2013).
evidence: This is based on a previously published crystal structure.

claim: All four human Argonautes likely recognize t1A nucleotides using the same mechanism.
source: We therefore suggest that all four human Argonautes likely recognize t1A nucleotides using the same mechanism.
evidence: This is inferred from the conservation of the t1-binding site residues and structural similarity.

claim: Some members of the Piwi clade of Argonaute proteins display t1-nucleotide preferences.
source: Additionally, recent studies indicate that some members of the Piwi clade of Argonaute proteins also display t1-nucleotide preferences.
evidence: This is based on recent studies in the field.

claim: Drosophila protein Aubergine preferentially cleaves targets bearing a t1A.
source: Specifically, the Drosophila protein Aubergine, the silkmoth protein Siwi, and the mouse protein Mili preferentially cleave targets bearing a t1A; while mouse protein Miwi2 prefers targets with a t1 purine (Wang et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: The silkmoth protein Siwi preferentially cleaves targets bearing a t1A.
source: Specifically, the Drosophila protein Aubergine, the silkmoth protein Siwi, and the mouse protein Mili preferentially cleave targets bearing a t1A; while mouse protein Miwi2 prefers targets with a t1 purine (Wang et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: The mouse protein Mili preferentially cleaves targets bearing a t1A.
source: Specifically, the Drosophila protein Aubergine, the silkmoth protein Siwi, and the mouse protein Mili preferentially cleave targets bearing a t1A; while mouse protein Miwi2 prefers targets with a t1 purine (Wang et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: Mouse protein Miwi2 prefers targets with a t1 purine.
source: Specifically, the Drosophila protein Aubergine, the silkmoth protein Siwi, and the mouse protein Mili preferentially cleave targets bearing a t1A; while mouse protein Miwi2 prefers targets with a t1 purine (Wang et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: Most Piwi proteins displaying t1 preferences have conserved residues lining the t1-binding site.
source: We note that most Piwi proteins displaying t1 preferences have conserved residues lining the t1-binding site (with the notable exception of Mili, which appears to lack several residues homologous to the t1A-binding residues in Ago2).
evidence: This is based on sequence alignment analysis.

claim: Mili appears to lack several residues homologous to the t1A-binding residues in Ago2.
source: We note that most Piwi proteins displaying t1 preferences have conserved residues lining the t1-binding site (with the notable exception of Mili, which appears to lack several residues homologous to the t1A-binding residues in Ago2).
evidence: This is based on sequence alignment analysis.

claim: Drosophila and silkmoth Ago3 do not display t1 preferences.
source: In contrast, Drosophila and silkmoth Ago3, which do not display t1 preferences (Wang et al., 2014), lack homology in key residues making up the t1-binding pocket (Figure 7).
evidence: This is supported by a citation and sequence alignment analysis.

claim: Drosophila and silkmoth Ago3 lack homology in key residues making up the t1-binding pocket.
source: In contrast, Drosophila and silkmoth Ago3, which do not display t1 preferences (Wang et al., 2014), lack homology in key residues making up the t1-binding pocket (Figure 7).
evidence: This is based on sequence alignment analysis.

claim: Both t1A and t1U nucleotides are conserved features of many miRNA target sites in C. elegans.
source: In C. elegans, both t1A and t1U nucleotides are conserved features of many miRNA target sites, indicating that the Argonaute proteins Alg-1 and Alg-2 also have t1 nucleotide preferences (Jan et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: The Argonaute proteins Alg-1 and Alg-2 in C. elegans have t1 nucleotide preferences.
source: In C. elegans, both t1A and t1U nucleotides are conserved features of many miRNA target sites, indicating that the Argonaute proteins Alg-1 and Alg-2 also have t1 nucleotide preferences (Jan et al., 2011).
evidence: This is inferred from the conservation of t1A and t1U in C. elegans miRNA target sites.

claim: There are only two minor differences between residues making up the human Ago2 t1-binding pocket and the equivalent residues in Alg-1 and Alg-2.
source: Curiously, there are only two minor differences between residues making up the human Ago2 t1-binding pocket and the equivalent residues in Alg-1 and Alg-2 (Asn-429 and Arg-479 in Ago2).
evidence: This is based on sequence alignment analysis.

claim: Substitutions in Alg-1 and Alg-2 could reorganize the t1-pocket water network to recognize both adenine and uracil nucleobases.
source: Conceivably, these substitutions could reorganize the t1-pocket water network to recognize both adenine and uracil nucleobases.
evidence: This is a speculative inference about how Alg-1 and Alg-2 might recognize both t1A and t1U.

claim: Alg-1 and Alg-2 may specifically bind t1A, and conservation of miRNA sites with t1U may be connected to recognition by other C. elegans Argonaute proteins.
source: Alternatively, we suggest that Alg-1 and Alg-2 may specifically bind t1A, and that conservation of miRNA sites with t1U is connected to recognition by one or more of the other C. elegans Argonaute proteins.
evidence: This is an alternative speculative hypothesis about t1 recognition in C. elegans.

claim: Understanding the t1-binding site may provide new inroads for development of novel anti-miR oligonucleotides.
source: Finally, we suggest that understanding the t1-binding site may provide new inroads for development of novel anti-miR oligonucleotides (van Rooij and Kauppinen, 2014).
evidence: This is a speculative suggestion about potential applications of the findings.

claim: The addition of a t1DAP nucleotide increased target affinity fourfold compared to non-t1A targets.
source: We found that the addition of a t1DAP nucleotide increased target affinity fourfold compared to non-t1A targets (Table 2).
evidence: This is supported by binding experiments reported in Table 2.

claim: The t1-binding pocket is spacious enough to accommodate nucleotide analogues much more elaborate than DAP.
source: More importantly, the t1-binding pocket has a chemically diverse surface and is spacious enough to accommodate nucleotide analogues much more elaborate than DAP.
evidence: This is inferred from the structural analysis of the t1-binding pocket.

claim: Displacement of ordered water molecules A and B may lead to entropic gains that translate into higher binding affinity.
source: Moreover, displacement of ordered water molecules A and B may lead to entropic gains that translate into higher binding affinity, in a fashion similar to that used in the development of cyclic urea HIV-1 protease inhibitors (Lam et al., 1994).
evidence: This is a speculative inference based on analogy to HIV-1 protease inhibitor development.

claim: t1-nucleotide analogs that make favorable contacts inside the t1-binding pocket could lead to anti-miRs that specifically target the Argonaute-miRNA complex.
source: We suggest that t1-nucleotide analogs that make favorable contacts inside the t1-binding pocket could lead to anti-miRs that specifically target the Argonaute-miRNA complex.
evidence: This is a speculative suggestion about potential therapeutic applications.
